prize_parts.citation: for showing, with transparent empirical designs, how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, job polarisation and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration changed in this round. I keep B009 as the single part, but I now prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson to my round-1 trio of Autor, Hanson and Katz. Three things moved me. First, the exchange showed that the real choice is the definition of the discovery, and I think the better-bounded discovery is the empirical evidence on how technology and trade reshape local labour demand. Dorn is a full co-author of the China-shock papers, and Autor and Dorn (2013) is itself a task-and-polarisation paper. So this trio covers both strands with named authors, and Autor remains the bridge. Second, Dreber Almenberg's point that Katz's best-known work on education and technology is closely tied to Goldin's research, which was recognised in 2023, is a real marginal-credit problem. It sits close to the overlap I flagged in round 1. Katz also appears in B050, which the committee has not settled. Third, the Dorn trio rests on designs that outside researchers have re-run, and the core finding of large, persistent local adjustment costs has survived a decade of scrutiny, although magnitudes are debated. The work is mature, with foundational papers from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s. It has shaped how policymakers and the public understand displacement from technology and globalisation. The citation is deliberately empirical. It does not claim the task-based theory of automation, whose other originators (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) are not credited, and it does not claim the skill-premium literature as a whole. I do not treat the first-place counts or the five-versus-two split on the third name as evidence of merit. I changed because of the attribution argument.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this narrows the prize. Katz anchors the long-run supply-and-demand evidence on the skill premium, which is older and better confirmed than the trade-shock magnitudes. Dropping him puts more weight on the part of the work where shift-share inference, persistence and external validity are still debated. The wage-structure strand then goes uncredited, and five members, including my own round-1 self, judged it central. Omitting Katz is a real cost of the three-name cap. The technology and trade strands may also be two discoveries bundled into one citation. The 2023 and 2024 prizes are adjacent in theme, and the committee has described what they recognised in somewhat different terms. B014 has a more compact core and a cleaner pair of names, but it has uncredited priority claims and a contested size of welfare gains. B040 has concentrated attribution and full maturity, but I now think its identification is weaker and its overlap with the 2024 institutions prize is closer.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson because Katz's education-and-technology work is closely tied to Goldin's 2023 prize, and because Dorn's polarisation work lets a broad citation cover both strands.
responses.response: I find this persuasive and it is the main reason I changed. In round 1 I treated the overlap with 2023 as thematic, but for Katz it is closer, because the marginal credit sits next to work already recognised. I agree with your qualification that a trade-shock-only citation would understate the polarisation strand, so I kept the citation broad. I hold one reservation: Dorn's coverage of the technology strand is thinner than Katz's coverage of long-run skill supply and demand, and that cost remains.

responses.point: Teorell centres B009 on the China shock with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He argues this credits one identifiable discovery exactly and avoids the contested task-framework boundary.
responses.response: I now come close to your attribution, and I thank you for pressing it. Your argument that the trade-shock evidence can be credited exactly to its three authors, while the wage-structure tradition has more contributors, held up against the objections raised in round 1. I would differ slightly on wording. I would not limit the citation to import competition, because Autor and Dorn's polarisation work belongs to the same empirical programme. I take the narrower framing as the defensible one if the committee wants one clean discovery, and I would not claim it is clearly superior to the Katz version.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Katz because a citation spanning technology, trade and wage inequality needs the anchor of the skill supply-and-demand evidence. He says the narrow China-shock variant rests on a less settled base.
responses.response: That is the strongest argument against my change, and I do not dismiss it. The skill-premium evidence is older and better confirmed than the trade-shock magnitudes. My reply is that the question is what is left to credit. Katz's best-known contributions run through the Goldin research recognised in 2023, and a citation that depends on them invites the overlap you yourself called an attribution complication. I also agree with your point that B040 identification is weaker than B009. That is why B040 stays only an alternative for me, now behind B014.

responses.point: Enflo keeps Katz because without him the prize shrinks to a trade-exposure result and Autor becomes the only bridge to the technology strand. She would not oppose the Dorn trio if the committee decides the trade shock is the primary discovery.
responses.response: I take the bridge concern seriously, and my citation is drafted to address it by naming job polarisation as well as local labour-market adjustment. Your conditional openness to the Dorn trio matters, but I do not count it as a preference, as the chair summary also stated. I agree with you that the citation should say plainly that the three-name limit shaped the choice. It should also say that the wage-structure literature, including Katz's role, is not diminished by it.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B014 because the credited discovery is a single framework. He says B009 combines two strands whose credit is hard to put in one citation, and he refuses to defer to first-place counts.
responses.response: I agree that count-based deference is not evidence of merit, and I do not rely on it. Your bundling objection is fair, and the Dorn trio answers it in part because the three are co-authors across both strands. B014 is the closest rival. Priority claims (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) and the size of the selection welfare gains qualify the citation without defeating it, and a citation limited to selection and reallocation is a sensible response. I still rank B009 higher because its evidence comes from clearer, replicated designs and its policy relevance is more direct, but the gap is not large.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the discovery as the empirical evidence on technology, polarisation and trade-induced local adjustment (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) or the broader wage-structure account (Autor, Hanson, Katz). I changed on this question, and I could be wrong about where the marginal credit lies.
How much of the Katz strand is already covered by the 2023 prize, and how much of the technology territory the 2024 prize covers. Members have described these prizes differently.
The magnitude, persistence and external validity of the China-shock estimates, including the inference properties of shift-share exposure designs.
Whether the technology and trade strands are one achievement or two, and whether a narrower citation would be a better-bounded prize than B014.
Whether B014's priority and welfare-gain issues are easier to resolve than B009's Dorn-or-Katz choice. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from my supplied profile. My documented connections are co-authorship and IIES ties to committee colleagues Krusell, Boppart and Friberg (the last through the IJIO menu-costs paper with Ellingsen), and none of them is a credited name on the shortlist. Krusell's own work on technology and wage inequality is in the literature adjacent to B009. That is a disclosed field proximity and not a tie to a candidate. My round-1 note about a possible Stockholm proximity of some B040 candidates is not documented in my profile, so it is an unverified concern. B040 is now only an alternative and this concern played no part in the change from Katz to Dorn. As chair I also report that my chair summary describes stated positions only. All of this is disclosed and not adjudicated, and I claim no independent verification.
